name: Hardy Woodward Hunter
bio: Hardy Woodward Hunter was a student at Tennessee A&I in Nashville and part of the 1960 lunch-counter sit-in movement. After a white youth yanked him from his stool at a downtown counter, it was Hunter — not his attacker — who was charged with disorderly conduct and fined $100.
charges: Disorderly conduct / fighting — a Nashville lunch-counter sit-in

name: A. D. King
bio: The Rev. A. D. King — Alfred Daniel King, younger brother of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. — was one of 79 people arrested in March 1960 in the sit-in demonstrations at a dozen Atlanta eating places, booked under Georgia's anti-trespass and breach-of-peace laws and its Anti-Mask Act.
charges: Anti-trespass / breach of peace / Anti-Mask Act — Atlanta sit-ins
sentence: Arrested in the Atlanta sit-in demonstrations

name: Charles Billups
affiliation: Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights
bio: The Rev. Charles Billups was a leader of the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights, arrested with Fred Shuttlesworth in Birmingham on March 31, 1960 on charges of aiding and abetting the lunch-counter sit-downs and vagrancy. On April 4 he was sentenced to 180 days in jail and fined $100.
charges: Aiding and abetting sit-downs; vagrancy — Birmingham
sentence: 180 days in jail and a $100 fine

name: Robert Edwin King
bio: The Rev. R. Edwin King, a white theological student, was jailed in Montgomery, Alabama in 1960 for attempting to dine with a Black companion at the Jefferson Davis Hotel. First given 10 days and a $200 fine, he was re-sentenced on July 13 to three months at hard labor and freed on bond pending appeal.
charges: Segregation / breach-of-peace law — an interracial dining protest
sentence: Three months at hard labor (on appeal)

name: Elroy Embry
bio: Elroy Embry was a Black student jailed with the white theological student R. Edwin King in Montgomery, Alabama in 1960 for attempting to eat together at the Jefferson Davis Hotel. He was sentenced to three months at hard labor and released on bond pending appeal.
charges: Segregation / breach-of-peace law — an interracial dining protest
sentence: Three months at hard labor (on appeal)

name: Barbara Broxton
bio: Barbara Broxton was a 20-year-old Florida A&M student arrested in the Tallahassee lunch-counter sit-ins on Feb. 20, 1960. She served 48 days in jail, choosing imprisonment over a fine in the CORE-led 'jail-no-bail' protest against segregation.
charges: Sit-in / unlawful assembly — Tallahassee lunch-counter protest

name: Patricia Stephens
bio: Patricia Stephens was a Florida A&M student and CORE organizer jailed in the 1960 Tallahassee lunch-counter sit-ins, where she helped pioneer the 'jail, not bail' tactic. Her widely circulated 'Letter from a Tallahassee Jail' became a touchstone of the student movement.
charges: Sit-in / unlawful assembly — Tallahassee lunch-counter protest

name: Clarence Senior
bio: Clarence Senior was an Atlanta college student jailed in 1960 for his part in the lunch-counter sit-in demonstrations. He challenged the constitutionality of the segregated court in which he was tried.
sentence: Jailed for the sit-ins; challenged the segregated court

name: Richard Frank Parker
bio: Richard Frank Parker was a white Florida State University student and the only white participant in the Negro lunch-counter sit-ins in Jacksonville, Florida. Jailed on a vagrancy charge for a 90-day term, he had his jaw broken by a segregationist while in custody; he was freed after serving 60 days following nationwide protest.
charges: Vagrancy — joining the Jacksonville lunch-counter sit-ins

name: James A. Chance
bio: James A. Chance was a Native American man arrested for trespassing in Dunn, North Carolina in 1960 when he tried to enroll his children in an all-white school, in a desegregation challenge that swept up four adults and seven children.
charges: Trespassing — attempting to enroll his children in an all-white school

name: Lonnie C. King Jr.
affiliation: Committee on Appeal for Human Rights
bio: Lonnie C. King Jr. was a leader of the Atlanta student movement (the Committee on Appeal for Human Rights) who organized the October 1960 department-store sit-ins. He was arrested with Martin Luther King Jr. at Rich's Magnolia Room restaurant and tried for trespassing.
charges: State anti-trespass law — Atlanta department-store sit-in

name: Carolyn Long
bio: Carolyn Long was a 20-year-old Clark College student and a spokesman for the sit-in group seated at Rich's restaurant during the October 1960 Atlanta department-store demonstrations, among the 73 arrested who refused to leave the whites-only counters.
charges: State anti-trespass law — Atlanta department-store sit-in

name: Langston Goldfinch
bio: Langston Goldfinch was a white Tulane graduate student arrested at a McCrory's lunch counter in New Orleans in September 1960 while sitting with three Black students. He was charged with criminal anarchy under Louisiana's sedition statute — facing up to ten years — along with criminal mischief and conspiracy.
charges: Criminal anarchy (Louisiana sedition statute), criminal mischief, conspiracy — a lunch-counter sit-in
convicted: Indicted; freed on bond awaiting trial
sentence: Faced up to 10 years; challenged the sedition law

name: Patricia Ann Shuttlesworth
bio: Patricia Ann Shuttlesworth, a teenage daughter of the Rev. Fred Shuttlesworth, was hauled off a Greyhound bus and jailed in Gadsden, Alabama in 1960 for 'breach of the peace' after she sat in the front of the segregated bus while returning from an integrated youth camp. She was convicted of delinquency and placed on indefinite probation.
charges: 'Breach of the peace' / juvenile delinquency — sitting in the front of a segregated bus

name: Ruby Fredericka Shuttlesworth
bio: Ruby Fredericka Shuttlesworth, a daughter of the Rev. Fred Shuttlesworth, was arrested and jailed with her sister and brother in Gadsden, Alabama in 1960 for 'breach of the peace' after they sat in the front of a segregated Greyhound bus. She was convicted of juvenile delinquency and placed on indefinite probation.
charges: 'Breach of the peace' / juvenile delinquency — sitting in the front of a segregated bus

name: Fred Shuttlesworth Jr.
bio: Fred Shuttlesworth Jr., the young son of the Rev. Fred Shuttlesworth, was hauled off a Greyhound bus and jailed with his sisters in Gadsden, Alabama in 1960 for 'breach of the peace' after the children sat in the front of the segregated bus returning from an integrated youth camp. He was convicted of delinquency and placed on indefinite probation.
charges: 'Breach of the peace' / juvenile delinquency — sitting in the front of a segregated bus

name: Medgar Evers
bio: Medgar Evers was the NAACP field secretary for Mississippi and the state's foremost civil-rights organizer. In 1960 he was cited for contempt of court for publicly calling a court sentencing a 'gross miscarriage of justice' — a prosecution aimed at silencing his criticism of Mississippi's segregated courts. He was assassinated in 1963.
charges: Contempt of court — criticizing a sentencing as a 'gross miscarriage of justice'
